text: To run it, Rockefeller and the trustees chose William Rainey Harper.
He had earned a doctorate from Yale at nineteen, in Semitic languages, and he taught Hebrew with a kind of fame that was unusual for a scholar.
He was a Baptist, ambitious, and in a hurry.
He stayed in a hurry his whole life.
He drove himself without rest, and he died in office in 1906, of cancer, at forty-nine, fifteen years into the job.
He and his wife are buried in the chapel on the campus he built.
And he had a model in mind.

A generation earlier, Johns Hopkins had opened in Baltimore as the first true research university in the country, built on the German idea that a university should not just teach old books but produce new knowledge.
Harper wanted that for Chicago, and he wanted it bigger.
He did not want a quiet college.
He wanted graduate study and laboratories, a university press, and a faculty of stars, and he wanted it all at once, on day one.
He built things into the place that were strange for the time.
The university was coeducational from the start, admitting women alongside men.
He split the calendar into four quarters and kept the doors open year round, so a student could enroll in summer and graduate whenever the work was done.
He started the University of Chicago Press, which began publishing scholarly books and journals in 1892 and is still running.
He built an extension division to carry university classes out to working adults across the city.
